episode_title: Multiple Linear Regression I: Building the Regression Plane — Episode 1 of 2

cast.name: Maya
cast.style: Clear, curious, and measured explanatory delivery.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.style: Calm, precise, and conversational analytical delivery.

scenes.dialogue: Welcome to Regression Modeling Walkthrough. This episode begins Chapter 3, Multiple Linear Regression I. The central shift is simple but powerful. Instead of asking how one explanatory variable relates to a response, we ask how several explanatory variables work jointly. The chapter develops least squares regression planes, coefficient interpretation, model assumptions, goodness of fit, statistical inference for one coefficient, added variable plots, partial correlations, binary variables, transformations, and interaction terms.

The chapter emphasizes that linear regression is linear in its parameters, not necessarily linear in the explanatory variables. That distinction opens a large family of models. A fitted model can include logarithms, powers, binary indicators, and products of variables, while remaining a linear regression model in the coefficients. We will use the term life insurance example as a recurring thread, then turn to refrigerator prices and several specialized actuarial and financial applications.

The chapter starts with a demand-side question for term life insurance. Life insurance companies want to know who purchases insurance and how much they purchase. The data come from the Survey of Consumer Finances, a nationally representative survey with information on assets, liabilities, income, and demographic characteristics. The initial sample includes 500 households with positive incomes interviewed in 2004, and the analysis focuses on 275 families that purchased term life insurance.

For these families, the response is FACE, the policy face amount paid in the event of the named insured's death. Important characteristics include annual INCOME, years of EDUCATION for the survey respondent, and NUMHH, the number of household members. The chapter often works with LNFACE and LNINCOME, the natural logarithmic transformations of face amount and income. Those transformations help address strongly right-skewed distributions and reveal a relationship that is more readily approximated with a line.

Our goal is not merely to repeat formulas. We will follow the chapter's reasoning: inspect variables individually, inspect pairwise relationships, recognize the limitations of pairwise summaries, fit a regression plane by least squares, and then interpret the resulting coefficients while holding the other explanatory variables fixed. By the end of this first episode, the mechanics and meaning of the multiple linear regression model should be firmly in place.

script.segment_name: 3.1 Method of Least Squares and Data Summaries

scenes.dialogue: In the general setup there are k explanatory variables, one response variable, and a sample of size n. Observation i is the row consisting of x sub i 1 through x sub i k, together with y sub i. Thus each entity contributes k plus 1 measurements. In the term life application, k equals 3: EDUCATION, NUMHH, and LNINCOME explain LNFACE. With n equal to 275 households, the data consist of four measurements for each household.

The first instruction is to examine each variable in isolation. Table 3.1 reports means, medians, standard deviations, minima, and maxima. FACE has mean 747,581 and median 150,000. INCOME has mean 208,975 and median 65,000. In both cases, the mean greatly exceeds the median, suggesting right skewness. LNFACE has mean 11.990 and standard deviation 1.871. LNINCOME has mean 11.149 and standard deviation 1.295.

Scatter plots then reveal the relationship between an explanatory variable and the response. The plot of FACE versus INCOME has a large lower-left cluster, because many households have both small incomes and small insurance face amounts. Both variables are skewed, and their joint pattern is highly nonlinear. When the same values are expressed as LNFACE and LNINCOME, the plot suggests a relationship that can be approximated with a line, though it remains variable.

Because the observations are multivariate, a scatterplot matrix is useful. Each square displays one variable against another: the row determines the vertical axis and the column determines the horizontal axis. The chapter presents a half scatterplot matrix, displaying lower-left elements only. A corresponding correlation matrix gives numerical summaries. For example, the correlation of LNFACE with NUMHH is 0.288, with EDUCATION is 0.383, and with LNINCOME is 0.482.

But correlation measures only linear pairwise relationships. A correlation table may miss a nonlinear association visible in a scatterplot matrix. More importantly, neither a scatterplot matrix nor a correlation matrix quantifies joint relationships among several explanatory variables. This limitation motivates multiple regression. The evidence suggests that EDUCATION, NUMHH, and LNINCOME may each help explain LNFACE individually. The next step is to study their joint effect.

Geometrically, a line becomes a plane when more variables are introduced. The algebraic equation is y equals b sub 0 plus b sub 1 x sub 1 through b sub k x sub k. This defines a plane in k plus 1 dimensions. The chapter can display a three-dimensional graph with LNFACE as the response and EDUCATION and LNINCOME as explanatory variables, holding NUMHH fixed. Beyond three dimensions, meaningful graphical displays become difficult.

Usually, there are many more observations than the k plus 1 observations needed to determine a plane. So it is generally impossible to find one plane passing through every observation. Least squares chooses the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared vertical deviations: SS of b star equals the sum from i equals 1 to n of y sub i minus the proposed fitted value, squared. The selected coefficients are the least squares estimates.

Once the minimizing estimates are found, the fitted regression plane is written y hat equals b sub 0 plus b sub 1 x sub 1 through b sub k x sub k. For the term life data, the fitted plane is LNFACE hat equals 2.584 plus 0.206 times EDUCATION plus 0.306 times NUMHH plus 0.494 times LNINCOME. Every coefficient has an interpretation conditional on the other included explanatory variables.

The chapter notes that statistical and spreadsheet software routinely perform the numerical minimization. That availability lets analysts concentrate on the estimation ideas rather than calculation details. Still, matrix notation gives an explicit formula and clarifies the structure. The response vector y is an n by 1 column vector. The explanatory-variable matrix X is n by k plus 1, with a column for the intercept and columns for the explanatory variables.

For the intercept, the variable x sub i 0 is usually identically one. In the term life example, y is the vector of LNFACE values, and X contains a leading column of ones followed by EDUCATION, NUMHH, and LNINCOME. The first displayed observation has LNFACE equal to 9.904, corresponding to a face amount of 20,000 dollars, with 16 years of education, three household members, and logarithmic income 10.669, corresponding to 43,000 dollars.

Writing the parameter vector as b star, the sum of squares becomes the transpose of y minus X b star, multiplied by y minus X b star. Taking derivatives and setting them equal to zero yields the normal equations: X prime X b equals X prime y. If explanatory variables are not linear combinations of one another, X prime X is invertible. Then the unique least squares solution is b equals inverse of X prime X, times X prime y.

For term life, that matrix calculation produces the coefficient vector with entries 2.584, 0.206, 0.306, and 0.494. The important practical message is that multiple regression does not abandon the least squares principle from simple regression. It generalizes it. Instead of fitting the best line through a cloud of points, it fits the plane, or higher-dimensional linear surface, that minimizes the total squared residual variation.

script.segment_name: 3.2 Regression Model, Interpretation, and Estimator Properties

scenes.dialogue: Section 3.2 distinguishes the fitted regression plane from the regression model. The regression function is E y equals beta sub 0 x sub 0 plus beta sub 1 x sub 1 through beta sub k x sub k. Usually x sub 0 equals 1, so beta sub 0 is the intercept. It is the expected response when all explanatory variables equal zero. Although that value is often not substantively interesting, the intercept sets the height of the regression plane.

For a continuous explanatory variable x sub j, beta sub j is the expected change in y per unit change in x sub j, assuming the other explanatory variables are held fixed. The chapter initially describes this where x sub j varies continuously and is not related to the other explanatory variables. In calculus language, beta sub j is the partial derivative of E y with respect to x sub j. Holding the other variables fixed is essential to the interpretation.

Consider the signs in the fitted term life model. The NUMHH coefficient is 0.306, which is positive. Comparing households with the same income and education, the larger household is expected to demand more term life insurance. The chapter calls this sensible because larger households have more dependents for whom insurance can provide financial assets after a breadwinner's death. LNINCOME also has a positive coefficient, 0.494.

The EDUCATION coefficient is 0.206 and is also positive. Other things equal, more education is associated with a higher expected logarithmic face amount. To interpret its magnitude, the chapter holds NUMHH and LNINCOME at sample averages and lets EDUCATION increase from 14 to 14.1, 14.2, and 14.3 years. Fitted LNFACE increases by 0.0206 for each one-tenth-year increase, because 0.206 times 0.1 equals 0.0206.

Exponentiating fitted logarithmic face amounts converts predictions back to dollar face amounts. In the table, fitted FACE rises from 144,803 to 147,817, then 150,893, then 154,034. The percentage change for each 0.1-year step is approximately 2.08 percent. The chapter relates this to calculus: a small change in the logarithmic value of y is approximately a small proportional change in y. This is why natural logs are useful in regression interpretation.

For LNINCOME, a 0.1-unit increase in logarithmic income corresponds in the displayed table to a 10.52 percent increase in INCOME. The fitted FACE amount rises by 5.06 percent. The ratio is 0.482, close to the estimated coefficient 0.494. Thus, holding NUMHH and EDUCATION fixed, a one percent increase in income is associated with approximately a 0.482 percent increase in fitted FACE. This coefficient is called an elasticity.

Mathematically, elasticity is the derivative of log y with respect to log x. It is the ratio of the percentage change in one variable to the percentage change in another. The distinction matters: when both response and explanatory variable appear in natural logarithms, a coefficient has a percentage-change interpretation. When only the response is logged, a small coefficient can be interpreted as an approximate proportional change in the unlogged response for a unit change in the explanatory variable.

The chapter gives equivalent observables and error representations of the model. In the observables representation, the expected response is linear, explanatory variables are nonstochastic, responses have common variance sigma squared, responses are independent, and responses are normally distributed. In the error representation, y sub i equals the regression function plus epsilon sub i; errors have mean zero and variance sigma squared, are independent, and are normally distributed.

To motivate nonstochastic explanatory variables and independent responses, the chapter describes a stratified sampling basis. Each unique explanatory-variable combination can be treated as a stratum, and a random sample of responses is drawn from the relevant population. Responses within and across strata are independent. The chapter also cautions that the error representation emphasizes additive errors and can obscure the sampling basis, whereas the observables representation focuses on variables of interest.

Under assumptions F1 through F4, the least squares estimator b is unbiased for the parameter vector beta. In matrix form, E of y equals X beta. Substituting into b equals inverse of X prime X times X prime y shows that E of b equals beta. In particular, E of b sub j equals beta sub j. Unbiasedness means that across repeated sampling under the model, the estimator is centered at the true parameter.

Under the same assumptions, the variance of b is sigma squared times inverse of X prime X. Independence supplies zero covariance between distinct responses, and equal variance gives Var y equal to sigma squared I, where I is the identity matrix. The diagonal elements of Var b give the variances of individual coefficient estimates; off-diagonal elements give covariances between estimates. These facts later support standard errors and statistical inference.

The Gauss-Markov theorem adds a precision result. Among estimators that are linear functions of the responses, the least squares estimator is the minimum variance unbiased estimator of beta, assuming F1 through F4. Under the additional normality assumption F5, b is normally distributed. The reason is that b is a linear combination of normally distributed responses. That normality result underpins the inferential procedures developed later in the chapter.

Beyond the regression coefficients, the model contains sigma squared, the variance around the regression function. The chapter estimates it using residuals. The error epsilon sub i is y sub i minus the unobserved expected value. A residual e sub i is y sub i minus fitted y sub i. Residuals are estimated errors: they measure the observed response after subtracting the value predicted by the fitted regression plane.

The mean square error is s squared equals one divided by n minus k plus 1, multiplied by the sum of squared residuals. Its positive square root, s, is the residual standard deviation. It is also called the standard error of the estimate. The denominator is not n because fitting k plus 1 coefficients creates dependencies among residuals. In particular, the average residual is zero, leaving only n minus k plus 1 unrestricted residuals.

There must also be at least k plus 2 observations to observe variation about the fitted plane. With exactly k plus 1 observations, a plane can fit the data perfectly. For one explanatory variable, two points determine a line, so at least three observations are required to see deviation from that line. The denominator adjustment compensates for the reduced residual variability and makes s squared an unbiased estimator of sigma squared.

Goodness of fit is described through a partition of variation. Total sum of squares is the sum of squared deviations of y from its mean. For each observation, total deviation equals unexplained deviation, y minus y hat, plus explained deviation, y hat minus y bar. After squaring and summing, Total SS equals Error SS plus Regression SS. Least squares makes the cross-product terms sum to zero.

The coefficient of determination is R squared, defined as Regression SS divided by Total SS. It is interpreted as the proportion of variability explained by the regression function. The chapter also notes that R squared is the square of the correlation between y and fitted y. Its positive square root, R, is the multiple correlation coefficient: the correlation between the response and the best linear combination of the explanatory variables.

The ANOVA table organizes this decomposition. Regression has Regression SS, k degrees of freedom, and Regression MS. Error has Error SS, n minus k plus 1 degrees of freedom, and MSE. Total has Total SS and n minus 1 degrees of freedom. Mean squares are sums of squares divided by their degrees of freedom. In particular, MSE equals Error SS divided by n minus k plus 1, which is s squared.

A limitation of ordinary R squared is that it never decreases when an explanatory variable is added, even if that variable is useless. The adjusted coefficient of determination addresses this. R sub a squared equals one minus Error SS divided by n minus k plus 1, over Total SS divided by n minus 1. Equivalently, it is one minus s squared divided by s sub y squared. Better fit means smaller s squared and larger adjusted R squared.

For the term life regression of LNFACE on EDUCATION, NUMHH, and LNINCOME, Regression SS is 328.47, Error SS is 630.43, and Total SS is 958.90. The regression degrees of freedom are 3, error degrees of freedom are 271, and total degrees of freedom are 274. MSE is 2.326, so the residual standard deviation is 1.525.

The unadjusted R squared is 34.3 percent, calculated as 328.47 divided by 958.90. Without the explanatory variables, the typical error in logarithmic face amount would be s sub y equal to 1.871. Using EDUCATION, NUMHH, and LNINCOME reduces the typical error to 1.525. The adjusted R squared is 33.6 percent. These summaries show an improvement while also making clear that substantial variation remains unexplained.

This completes the foundation for Episode 1. We have moved from a multivariate dataset to a fitted regression plane, interpreted coefficients conditionally, stated the assumptions that support least squares properties, and measured residual variation and goodness of fit. In Episode 2, we turn to statistical inference, the refrigerator example, added variable plots, partial correlations, binary indicators, transformations, interactions, piecewise linear models, and the chapter exercises.

Before continuing, practice saying the model aloud: expected y equals an intercept plus a coefficient times each explanatory variable. Then add the key phrase: holding the other explanatory variables fixed. Practice distinguishing an error from a residual, and distinguish R squared from adjusted R squared. Finally, remember the least squares objective: choose coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals. Those ideas organize everything that follows.

That is Episode 1 of 2, Multiple Linear Regression I: Building the Regression Plane. In the next episode, we will ask whether individual variables are important, learn why pairwise correlation can conflict with a regression coefficient, and see how binary variables and interactions expand the regression framework. Thanks for listening to Regression Modeling Walkthrough.
